text: Live now: Nasser al-Kidwa, former Palestinian Authority Foreign Minister, and Ehud Olmert, former Prime Minister of Israel, join Columbia Institute of Global Politics to discuss their proposal for a negotiated peace between Israelis and Palestinians.

sharedPost.text:
Columbia University’s Institute of Global Politics (IGP) will host Nasser al-Kidwa, former Palestinian Authority Foreign Minister, and Ehud Olmert, former Prime Minister of Israel, for a discussion about their proposal for a negotiated peace between Israelis and Palestinians. The conversation will be moderated by Secretary Jacob Lew. The discussion will examine the proposal’s political feasibility, and the implications of the recent ceasefire in Gaza, and President Trump’s 20 Point Plan.
Opening remarks will be delivered by Keren Yarhi-Milo, Dean of Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs and Adlai E. Stevenson Professor of International Relations. 

Speakers:
Nasser al-Kidwa, Former Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Palestinian National Authority

Ehud Olmert, Former Prime Minister of Israel (2006-2009)

Jacob Lew (moderator), Former US Ambassador to Israel, 76th US Secretary of the Treasury, Professor of International and Public Affairs and IGP Faculty Policy Director, Columbia SIPA

Introductory remarks by: 
Keren Yarhi-Milo, Dean of Columbia School of International and Public Affairs; Adlai E. Stevenson Professor of International Relations; IGP Cofounder and Faculty Advisory Board Member

text: Join Columbia Institute of Global Politics for a live discussion about today's complex trade environment and the challenges ahead.

sharedPost.text:
Join us for a timely Across the Aisle conversation on today’s complex trade environment and the challenges ahead. The discussion will feature two former US Trade Representatives from across the political spectrum—Ambassador Froman under President Obama and Ambassador Lighthizer under President Trump—sharing insights from their time at the negotiating table and reflecting on how to solve some of the toughest issues around trade, from navigating tariffs to building greater resilience in global supply chains to managing digital commerce. 

Speakers:

Mike Froman, 17th US Trade Representative (2013-2017) and President of the Council on Foreign Relations

Robert Lighthizer, 18th US Trade Representative (2017-2021)

Merit Janow (moderator), Dean Emerita, Professor of Practice in International Economic Law and International Affairs and IGP Affiliated Faculty Member, Columbia SIPA

Introductory remarks by:

Jacob Lew, Professor of International and Public Affairs, IGP Faculty Policy Director, and IGP Faculty Advisory Board Member, Columbia SIPA; 76th US Secretary of the Treasury

text: Take a look back at Columbia University Irving Medical Center's Hispanic Heritage Month celebration!

sharedPost.text:
Columbia University Irving Medical Center celebrated Hispanic Heritage Month on Oct. 9 with a lively celebration on Haven Plaza, uniting students, faculty, staff, and community members.

Hosted by the Office of Academic and Community Partnerships and the LatinX Employee Resource Group, the event highlighted Hispanic culture through food, music, and a performance by the Harold O. Levy School 52 marching band, in line with the national theme, “Collective Heritage: Honoring the Past, Inspiring the Future.”

Officials from the offices of Mayor Eric Adams and Governor Kathy Hochul also attended, presenting proclamations recognizing Oct. 1 as “Latino Physician Day” in New York City and State.

text: Columbia Law School announces a transformative gift.

sharedPost.text:
The multiyear project to fully reimagine Columbia Law School’s library took a momentous step forward thanks to a lead gift of $15 million from Li Lu LAW ’96, BUS ’96, CC ’96. In recognition of his exceptional level of support—no individual has made a larger single gift in the Law School’s history—the new space will be known as the Li Lu Law Library.

Born in China, Li Lu graduated from Columbia University in 1996, when he received a B.A., J.D., and MBA—becoming the first student to earn three degrees simultaneously. In 1997, he founded the value-investing firm Himalaya Capital, where he is chairman and continues to manage its principal fund. He is also co-founder and inaugural board chair of The Asian American Foundation.

💬 “My time at Columbia reinforced for me that a library is never just a building or collection. Rather, it is the intellectual heart of a university,” says Li Lu. “I believe great institutions must continually renew themselves. This gift is my way of helping Columbia Law School remain at the forefront of legal education here in the U.S. and around the world.”

💬 “The Li Lu Law Library will be a vibrant hub of intellectual activity and interpersonal connection,” says Dean Daniel Abebe. “Li Lu’s gift is an unprecedented investment in the student experience and ensures that Columbia Law School will continue to attract the most talented students and scholars, providing them with unparalleled resources for success. I am enormously grateful to Li Lu for his incredible generosity and unwavering commitment to the Law School.”

Scheduled to open later this fall, the Li Lu Law Library will serve as the Law School’s signature space for learning, collaborating, and community building. Learn more about Li Lu and his thoughts about the library: https://bit.ly/4q0V8uG

text: Join the Wallach Art Gallery for a special screening this Sunday, Oct. 19.

sharedPost.text:
To mark the final day of the exhibition "Homage: Queer lineages on video", join us October 19, from 1:00–2:00 pm, at the Lenfest Center for the Arts (615 West 129th Street) for a special screening of works by Luke Fowler (b. 1978) and Derek Jarman (1942-1994).

 
Fowler's recent film "Being Blue" (2025), shot during a residency at Prospect Cottage—Jarman's final home—will be shown along with two recently restored and digitized Super 8 films by Jarman, "Studio Bankside" (1971-1972) and "Sloane Square" (1976).

sharedPost.text:
BREAKING NEWS
The 2025 Nobel Prize in Literature is awarded to the Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai “for his compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art.”

The author László Krasznahorkai was born in 1954 in the small town of Gyula in southeast Hungary, near the Romanian border. A similar remote rural area is the scene of Krasznahorkai’s first novel ‘Sátántangó’, published in 1985 (‘Satantango’, 2012), which was a literary sensation in Hungary and the author’s breakthrough work. The novel portrays, in powerfully suggestive terms, a destitute group of residents on an abandoned collective farm in the Hungarian countryside just before the fall of communism. Silence and anticipation reign, until the charismatic Irimiás and his crony Petrina, who were believed by all to be dead, suddenly appear on the scene. To the waiting residents, they seem as messengers either of hope or of the last judgement. The satanic element referred to in the title of the book is present in their slave morality and in the pretences of the trickster Irimiás which, effective as they are deceitful, leave almost all of them tied up in knots. Everyone in the novel is waiting for a miracle to happen, a hope that is from the very outset punctured by the book’s introductory Kafka motto: ‘In that case, I’ll miss the thing by waiting for it.’ The novel was made into a highly original 1994 film in collaboration with the director Béla Tarr.

The American critic Susan Sontag soon crowned Krasznahorkai contemporary literature’s ‘master of the apocalypse’, a judgement she arrived at after having read the author’s second book ‘Az ellenállás melankóliája’ (1989; ‘The Melancholy of Resistance’, 1998). Here, in a feverish horror fantasy played out in a small Hungarian town nestled in a Carpathian valley, the drama has been heightened even further. From the very first page, we – together with the charmless Mrs Pflaum – find ourselves entering a dizzying state of emergency. Ominous signs abound. Crucial to the dramatic sequence of events is the arrival in the city of a ghostly circus, whose main attraction is the carcass of a giant whale. This mysterious and menacing spectacle sets extreme forces in motion, prompting the spread of both violence and vandalism. Meanwhile, the inability of the military to prevent anarchy creates the possibility of a dictatorial coup. Employing dreamlike scenes and grotesque characterisations, László Krasznahorkai masterfully portrays the brutal struggle between order and disorder. None may escape the effects of terror.

In the novel ‘Háború és háború’ (1999; War & War, 2006) Krasznahorkai shifts his attention beyond the borders of his Hungarian homeland in allowing the humble archivist Korin to decide, as his life’s final act, to travel from the outskirts of Budapest to New York such that he might, for a moment, take his place at the centre of the world. Back home in the archives, he has found an exceptionally beautiful ancient epic about returning warriors that he hopes to make known to the world. Krasznahorkai’s prose has developed towards the flowing syntax with long, winding sentences devoid of full stops that has become his signature.

Continue reading about the 2025 Nobel Prize in Literature: https://bit.ly/4pMBORJ

🏆 Congratulations to Kristina G. Douglass, archaeologist and Associate Professor of Climate at Columbia Climate School, who has been named a 2025 MacArthur Fellow. 

The "genius grant" from MacArthur Foundation recognizes exceptional creativity and dedication, celebrating creative potential through a no-strings-attached $800,000 fellowship.

Douglass investigates how human societies and environments have co-evolved and adapted to climate variability over time. Her research, based in southwest Madagascar, uses lessons from the past to understand how to adapt to climate change, working in close, longstanding collaborations with local and Indigenous communities.

Read more about Douglass and her work via Columbia Climate School's State of the Planet: https://news.climate.columbia.edu/2025/10/08/archaeologist-kristina-douglass-named-macarthur-fellow/

A Columbia dermatologist has developed ways to engineer other cells to find and eliminate the misguided B cells. If successful, the therapy could be adapted for many more autoimmune conditions.

🥳 Happy birthday, Alma Mater!  

Our iconic statue turns 122 today. Shown here at her unveiling ceremony in 1903, Alma Mater was designed by Daniel Chester French and cast by John Williams. In her early years, Alma Mater was gilded and glowed in the sunlight. 

Learn more about Alma Mater's arrival on Morningside campus: https://blogs.library.columbia.edu/outdoorsculpture/2014/07/15/unveiling-alma-mater/

🌍 Exciting news for Columbia GS! 

Columbia University and City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK) are expanding their partnership with the Joint Bachelor's Degree Program between City U and Columbia 🎓✨ Starting in Fall 2026, high school graduates can apply directly for the first time.

Students spend their first two years at CityUHK—named the Most International University in the World 2025 by Times Higher Education—before completing their studies at Columbia in New York City. Graduates earn two bachelor’s degrees and gain an unparalleled academic and cultural experience across two continents.

This program combines Columbia’s renowned Core Curriculum with CityUHK’s Discovery Enriched Curriculum, preparing students to thrive in an increasingly interconnected world.

Last week, the 10th Annual 'Back-2-School' Block Party was a celebration of community as families, organizations, and neighbors gathered to kick off the start of the new school year.✨  

NYPD 26th Precinct’s Community Affairs division, Manhattan Community Board 9, and the West Harlem Development Corporation—with support from Columbia Community Service, Columbia University Facilities and Operations’ Construction Business Initiatives unit, Columbia’s Office of Public Safety, and other local organizations—hosted a massive Manhattanville block party to distribute backpacks and school supplies to local youth, complete with face painting, games, and tunes spun by a local DJ.

Tap the 🔗 here to check out awesome photos and more of the event recap: https://bit.ly/41Ca3RA
 
📷: Michael DiVito

text:
🌳 College Walk will look a little different for the fall semester! 

Unfortunately, several of the older trees along the Morningside campus path were in declining health and presented a safety risk, and therefore needed to be removed. Working with leading arborists, our Grounds team developed a new look that honors the historic design of College Walk while looking toward Columbia’s future. 

The revamped design will highlight the flowering Kwanzan cherry blossom trees that have lived on College Walk for decades. Linden trees will remain at either end of the Walk, and seasonal plantings will bloom near the trees. This new arrangement will open up sightlines to better take in Morningside’s grand architecture. 

Another benefit of these changes: benches will be added around the perimeter of College Walk, adding plenty of additional seating and creating new spots to gather with friends. 

📷 Eileen Barroso
